title: From Shells to Screens: A Short History of Money
context:
Most of us were taught that money grew out of barter. According to this familiar story, early people swapped goods directly, and when this proved clumsy, since a shoemaker with a surplus of shoes might not find a baker who needed them, they began to use a common item such as shells or metal as a go-between. The tale is appealing, but anthropologists have found little evidence for it. No society has been discovered that depended mainly on barter between its own members. Instead, small communities typically relied on gifts, favours and informal credit, remembering who owed what to whom.

The earliest written records support this view. Around 3000 BCE, temple officials in Mesopotamia used clay tablets to record debts, mostly in barley, and fixed their value against a standard weight of silver. The silver itself rarely changed hands. It served as a unit of account, a way of comparing the worth of different goods, rather than as a means of payment. In other words, the idea of a measure of value seems to have preceded the invention of any physical currency.

Coins arrived much later. The kingdom of Lydia, in what is now Turkey, produced stamped lumps of a natural gold-and-silver alloy in the seventh century BCE. The stamp was the important feature. By guaranteeing weight and purity, the ruler spared buyers and sellers from having to weigh and test the metal at every transaction. Coins proved especially useful for paying armies, and the practice spread quickly across the Greek world. China developed its own tradition independently, casting bronze coins with a hole in the middle so that they could be strung together in bundles.

Heavy coins are inconvenient for large payments, which led to another innovation. In China, from about the ninth century CE, merchants began to leave their coins with trusted deposit shops in exchange for paper receipts that could be redeemed elsewhere. In the eleventh century the government took over the issue of paper notes. The result was a success until officials found that they could solve their financial problems by printing more, which caused prices to rise. Europe adopted paper money many centuries later, when goldsmiths and early banks began to issue notes promising to pay the bearer in precious metal on demand.

For a long time, a note's value was linked to a store of gold. The last connection was cut in 1971, when the United States stopped exchanging dollars for gold. Today most national currencies are fiat money, which has no intrinsic worth. It is valuable because the government declares it legal tender and agrees to accept it as payment for taxes, and above all because people expect others to accept it too. Money, in other words, works only as long as it is trusted.

That trust now attaches increasingly to numbers rather than objects. The majority of money exists only as entries in bank databases. In Kenya, a mobile phone service allows people with no bank account to send payments by text message, and it has become an important part of the economy. Cryptocurrencies, designed to function without any central authority, represent a more radical experiment, though their prices have fluctuated so wildly that few people use them for everyday purchases. Whatever form it takes, money is best understood not as a thing but as a shared belief, one which societies have found many ingenious ways to record.

questions.prompt: What problem with barter does the familiar story emphasise?
options: Goods could not be stored for long
Traders did not know the prices
Shells were too heavy to carry
It was hard to find someone who wanted what you offered
questions.answer: It was hard to find someone who wanted what you offered
questions.why: Thợ giày có giày dư có thể không tìm được người bán bánh cần giày.
questions.quote: might not find a baker who needed them

questions.prompt: What have anthropologists found?
options: Barter was the earliest form of trade in all societies
No society has been found that depended mainly on barter among its own members
Early communities had no idea of debt
Gifts were forbidden in early communities
questions.answer: No society has been found that depended mainly on barter among its own members
questions.why: Các nhà nhân học ít thấy bằng chứng cho câu chuyện hàng đổi hàng.
questions.quote: No society has been discovered that depended mainly on barter between its own members.

questions.prompt: What did small communities typically rely on?
options: Gifts, favours and informal credit
Shells and metals
Coins
Written contracts
questions.answer: Gifts, favours and informal credit
questions.why: Cộng đồng nhỏ dựa vào quà tặng, ơn huệ và tín dụng phi chính thức.
questions.quote: relied on gifts, favours and informal credit

questions.prompt: What did the Mesopotamian clay tablets record?
options: Sales made with silver coins
Taxes paid in shells
Debts, mostly in barley, valued against a silver standard
Payments made to soldiers
questions.answer: Debts, mostly in barley, valued against a silver standard
questions.why: Các tấm đất sét ghi nợ chủ yếu bằng lúa mạch, quy ra khối lượng bạc.
questions.quote: record debts, mostly in barley, and fixed their value against a standard weight of silver

questions.prompt: In paragraph 2, 'a unit of account' means
options: a coin stamped by a ruler
a way of comparing the worth of different goods
a record of who owes money
an official working in a temple
questions.answer: a way of comparing the worth of different goods
questions.why: Bài tự giải thích ngay sau đó.
questions.quote: a way of comparing the worth of different goods

questions.prompt: What does the Mesopotamian evidence suggest?
options: Coins existed before writing
Silver was the first physical currency
Temples forbade credit
The idea of a measure of value came before physical currency
questions.answer: The idea of a measure of value came before physical currency
questions.why: Ý niệm thước đo giá trị dường như có trước tiền vật chất.
questions.quote: the idea of a measure of value seems to have preceded the invention of any physical currency

questions.prompt: What was the important feature of the Lydian coins?
options: The stamp that guaranteed weight and purity
The fact that they were made of pure gold
Their round shape
The hole in the middle
questions.answer: The stamp that guaranteed weight and purity
questions.why: Dấu đóng của nhà cai trị bảo đảm trọng lượng và độ tinh khiết.
questions.quote: The stamp was the important feature.

questions.prompt: What benefit did stamped coins bring?
options: They were lighter than gold bars
They were impossible to copy
Buyers and sellers no longer had to weigh and test the metal each time
They could be strung together
questions.answer: Buyers and sellers no longer had to weigh and test the metal each time
questions.why: Dấu đóng giúp khỏi phải cân và kiểm kim loại ở mỗi giao dịch.
questions.quote: spared buyers and sellers from having to weigh and test the metal

questions.prompt: How did Chinese coins differ from those of Lydia?
options: They were made of a gold-and-silver alloy
They were cast in bronze with a hole so they could be strung
They were used only to pay soldiers
They were stamped to guarantee purity
questions.answer: They were cast in bronze with a hole so they could be strung
questions.why: Trung Quốc đúc tiền đồng có lỗ ở giữa để xâu thành chuỗi.
questions.quote: casting bronze coins with a hole in the middle

questions.prompt: What led to the use of paper receipts in China?
options: A shortage of bronze
Demand from the government
Trade with Europe
The inconvenience of heavy coins for large payments
questions.answer: The inconvenience of heavy coins for large payments
questions.why: Tiền xu nặng bất tiện cho thanh toán lớn nên thương nhân gửi tiền, nhận biên lai giấy.
questions.quote: Heavy coins are inconvenient for large payments

questions.prompt: What went wrong when the Chinese government issued paper notes?
options: Merchants refused to accept them
They were easily forged
Officials printed more to solve financial problems, which raised prices
They could not be exchanged for coins
questions.answer: Officials printed more to solve financial problems, which raised prices
questions.why: In thêm tiền gây tăng giá (lạm phát).
questions.quote: they could solve their financial problems by printing more, which caused prices to rise

options: They promised to pay the bearer in precious metal on demand
They were backed by land
They were issued directly by kings
They could be used only abroad
questions.answer: They promised to pay the bearer in precious metal on demand

options: Banks stopped issuing notes
The United States stopped exchanging dollars for gold
Gold coins were first minted
Paper money was introduced in Europe

questions.why: Mối liên hệ cuối cùng với vàng bị cắt năm 1971.
questions.quote: the United States stopped exchanging dollars for gold

questions.prompt: In paragraph 5, 'intrinsic worth' means
options: a high price
a legal status
an attractive design
value in itself, apart from what people agree to
questions.answer: value in itself, apart from what people agree to

options: The government declares it legal tender, accepts it for taxes, and people expect others to accept it
It is backed by gold
It is rare and hard to produce
It is difficult to copy
questions.answer: The government declares it legal tender, accepts it for taxes, and people expect others to accept it

It is based on cryptocurrency

options: They are illegal everywhere
Their prices have fluctuated wildly
They are too heavy to carry
They require a bank account

questions.why: Giá biến động quá mạnh.
questions.quote: their prices have fluctuated so wildly that few people use them for everyday purchases

questions.prompt: What is the writer's final claim about money?
options: It is a physical object
It is controlled by banks
Its form has never changed
It is best understood as a shared belief

To describe how shell money was used
To present a popular explanation and question it
To criticise anthropologists

options: As a chronological account that challenges a common story
As an argument in favour of cryptocurrencies
As a comparison of China and Europe
As a guide to investing
questions.answer: As a chronological account that challenges a common story
